# Flush Selective Retention on Non-Working Sessions

The memory-compiler flush stage normally emits `FLUSH_OK` — writing nothing to the daily log — when a session produced no durable knowledge. The 2026-08-05 flush demonstrates a middle case: a session that was explicitly "a data snapshot, not a working session," with no decisions and no lessons, but whose contents were nonetheless preserved because several items carried hard deadlines or closing windows. The flush wrote the items down *and* annotated why, making the retention decision auditable rather than implicit.

## Key Points

- **Two distinct retention criteria.** The default criterion is *knowledge durability* (did this session teach something reusable?). The 2026-08-05 flush applied a second, orthogonal criterion: *time sensitivity* (will this item expire or escalate if not surfaced?). An item can fail the first test and still pass the second.
- **The retention rationale was written into the log itself.** The flush appended an explicit note — "This was a data snapshot, not a working session — no decisions or lessons produced. The action items above are preserved only because several are time-sensitive" — so a downstream reader (or compiler) knows the entry is a deliberate exception, not a misclassification.
- **Non-decision content is labeled as such.** The action items were headed "surfaced for follow-up, not new decisions," preventing the compiler from later mistaking a triage snapshot for a decision record.
- **What qualified as time-sensitive:** a security alert, a counterparty's closing availability window (leave dates), and immediate signature/confirmation actions. Ordinary aging replies were included only as context around these.
- **Cost trade-off:** preserving a snapshot costs a small amount of daily-log volume; discarding one risks dropping a deadline entirely, since the snapshot has no other durable home once the session ends.

## Details

The flush stage sits at a lossy boundary: it reads a session transcript and decides what, if anything, survives into `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Its default posture is aggressive discard, because most session chatter is transient and the daily logs are the compiler's source of truth. But a purely knowledge-oriented filter has a blind spot — operational obligations. A triage snapshot contains no lesson, no decision, and no reusable pattern, so it fails a strict "durable knowledge" test, yet it may be the only artifact in the system holding a 3-day-old security alert or a leave window that closes in three days. Once the session closes and the transcript is archived, that obligation has no other retrieval path.

The 2026-08-05 flush resolved this by widening the retention test rather than relaxing it: the items were kept under an explicitly named second criterion, and the reasoning was recorded inline. This self-documenting exception is the transferable practice. It avoids two failure modes at once — silently dropping deadline-bearing content, and silently inflating the log with snapshots that a future reader would mistake for substantive work. The pattern parallels the triage-vs-execution split seen in the inbox-triage runs themselves: surfacing and categorizing is a distinct act from deciding, and labeling output as one or the other keeps the downstream consumer honest. It also complements the broader principle behind the on-ramp pipeline — keep material retrievable while keeping the standing context lean — by admitting only the subset whose expiry cost justifies the space.

# Scoped Commit in a Dirty Working Tree (dotclaude Repo)

When the 2026-09-19 hook fix landed in `~/.claude/settings.json`, the change was deliberately left uncommitted and handed to the user with an exact path-scoped command. The reason was the state of the surrounding working tree: `~/.claude` is the synced `erash11/dotclaude` repository, and it carried unrelated uncommitted work — a `UserPromptSubmit` skill-router hook from a separate thread, plus dirty session transcripts. Committing the repair required staging one file by path rather than the whole tree. The commit was finally made and pushed on 2026-09-23.

## Key Points

- **The prescribed command stages a single file:** `git -C ~/.claude add settings.json && git commit -m "Hooks: drop the unguarded Mac-path dcg duplicate" && git push`. The `-C` flag targets the repo without changing the working directory, and naming the path avoids sweeping in adjacent changes.
- **A dirty tree makes a blanket commit unsafe, not merely untidy.** In-flight work from another thread would be committed half-finished, and transcript churn would be pushed to a shared remote alongside a one-line config fix.
- **The commit was deferred to the user rather than performed** — the change touched a synced personal-config repo with third-party-authored pending work in it.
- **Deferral has a measured cost.** The handoff was not executed until 2026-09-23, four days later; in the interim the duplicate hook stayed in `HEAD`, the Mac kept double-firing, and one Windows session logged 49 `PreToolUse` errors before the fix was pushed.
- **Transcripts are routine noise in this repo.** Session records accumulate as working-tree changes continuously, so `~/.claude` is dirty by default — path-scoped commits are the normal mode there, not an exceptional accommodation.

## Details

The general rule this instance supports is that the appropriate staging granularity is a function of the repository's baseline cleanliness. In a project repo whose tree is clean between tasks, `git add -A` is a reasonable default and an unexpected extra file is itself a useful signal. In a configuration or state repo that is dirty as a matter of course — one holding transcripts, caches, machine-local scratch, or work from concurrent threads — the same command silently bundles unrelated content into every commit, destroying the history's usefulness for bisecting or reverting a specific change. `~/.claude` is squarely in the second category, which is why the remediation was written as an explicit single-path stage.

The deferral decision is separable from the scoping decision and rests on different grounds, and the 2026-09-23 outcome allows it to be graded. The repair itself was verified on 2026-09-19 — JSON validated, one hook remaining in the array, all 22 top-level keys intact, backup written — so the hesitation was not about correctness of the edit; it was about authority over a synced personal repo containing another thread's unfinished hook work. The risk recorded at the time was concrete and materialized: for four days `HEAD` carried a `settings.json` whose `PreToolUse` array ran `dcg` twice per tool call on the Mac and errored on every matching call on Windows. The lesson is that scoping and deferring are independent choices: path-scoping is what makes a commit safe in a dirty tree, and once the scoped command is known and the edit verified, deferring it further buys nothing while leaving the defect live on every synced host. See [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]] for the defect and its eventual push.

# Automation Stack Doctor and Self-Maintaining Scheduled-Task Cycle

The automation stack doctor is a health-check routine that verifies the full local Claude Code automation and memory stack — scheduled tasks, Python venvs, memsearch, Docker/Milvus, the error log, backups, and the Google Drive API heartbeat — and reports a consolidated status. On 2026-07-27, following a Windows reboot, a post-restart stack doctor run returned ALL CLEAR, and the session restructured the stack into a self-maintaining nightly cycle: heavy reindexing was moved into the 6:15 AM backup task while the session-end hook stays a light 45-second incremental pass.

## Key Points

- **Stack doctor scope:** a single run validates all 4 scheduled tasks, Python venvs, memsearch, Docker/Milvus survival across restart, error-log cleanliness, backup freshness, and a Google Drive API heartbeat. The 2026-07-27 post-restart run returned ALL CLEAR (backups fresh at 3h, Milvus survived reboot).
- **Self-deleting post-restart check:** a one-shot scheduled task (`KeystoneOS-PostRestartCheck`, triggered at logon + 5 min) auto-runs stack doctor after a reboot, escalates any failures to `.errors.log`, and deletes itself. This is the workaround for the fact that a session cannot literally wait through a machine restart — failures surface at the next session start via the error log.
- **Nightly reindex folded into the 6:15 AM backup task** (`daily-backup.ps1`): uncapped, uses the full `memsearch.exe` path (per the Task Scheduler PATH lesson), escalates per-path failures, and resets the hook timeout-streak counter on success. Rationale: a first-time SecondBrain book-library index is an hours-scale job that a 45-second session-end hook can never absorb.
- **Backup task execution limit raised 30 min → 2 h** so a heavy reindex night is not killed mid-pass. The session-end hook stays light (45 s incremental) and its alarm threshold was raised 3 → 6 so it only alarms if the nightly safety net itself falls behind — a real signal, not noise.
- **Cloud-check timezone bug fixed:** a "-4h old" false backup-freshness reading came from timestamps not normalized to UTC after `ConvertFrom-Json`; the check now normalizes to UTC regardless of the return type.

## Details

The session's central move is an architectural relocation of expensive work off the interactive/hook path and onto a scheduled job. The recurring memsearch indexing alarm had been misdiagnosed the prior day as an "occasional" hiccup; on 2026-07-27 it was recognized as structural — a first-time embedding job measured in hours (one indexer had burned 81 CPU-minutes and was still running). Because a 45-second session-end hook can never complete an hours-scale index, the correct home for that work is the nightly 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1` task, which runs uncapped and escalates per-path failures. The session-end hook is left as a light incremental pass, and its alarm threshold is raised from 3 to 6 consecutive misses so it only fires when the nightly safety net itself falls behind. With the library index converging over a night or two while search stays live, the alarm becomes a meaningful signal rather than chronic noise.

Two supporting reliability fixes accompanied the restructure. The backup task's execution time limit was raised from 30 minutes to 2 hours so a heavy reindex night is not terminated mid-pass — a scheduled job that runs an unbounded index needs an execution ceiling wide enough to absorb the worst case. # Windows `setx` Environment Variable Propagation Delay

On 2026-06-03, while setting `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` via `setx` to resolve a Claude Code `/doctor` warning, a new terminal tab opened inside VS Code still showed the old environment — despite `setx` having completed successfully. The root cause is a fundamental Windows process-model behavior: `setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately, but processes already running (and their children) retain a frozen copy of the environment from when they were launched.

## Key Points

- **`setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately** — the value appears in `HKCU\Environment` (for user-scoped vars) the moment the command returns. Any process launched fresh from Explorer, `Win + R`, or a standalone new terminal window will see the updated value.
- **Already-running processes are unaffected** — a running VS Code instance, its terminal tabs, its embedded Claude Code process, and any other child processes all inherited their environment snapshot at VS Code's launch time and cannot see values added via `setx` afterward.
- **New terminal tabs inside VS Code inherit VS Code's launch-time snapshot** — opening a new tab does not re-read the Windows registry. The child shell inherits the parent (VS Code) process's frozen environment, not the current registry state.
- **Fix: fully quit and reopen the parent application** — closing VS Code completely (File > Exit, confirming the process exits in Task Manager) and relaunching it causes it to spawn with the updated environment, which all child processes then inherit.
- **Per-session workaround without restart:** use `$env:VARNAME = "value"` in PowerShell or `export VARNAME=value` in bash within the current terminal. This sets the value for that shell process only (not persisted to registry) but takes effect immediately in that session.
- **Reuse existing PATs when scope matches** — on 2026-06-03, `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` already existed with sufficient GitHub scopes. Running `setx GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN <same-value>` reused that token rather than generating a redundant new PAT.

## Details

The `setx` command is the standard Windows mechanism for persisting environment variables across sessions — unlike `set` in CMD (current session only) or `$env:VARNAME = "value"` in PowerShell (current process only), `setx` writes to the Windows registry and makes the change available to all future processes. The critical constraint, however, is that qualifier: "future processes." The Windows process model gives each process an independent copy of the environment inherited from its parent at creation time. Modifying the registry does not broadcast changes to already-running processes — they continue indefinitely with their original snapshot.

VS Code is a particularly common trap for this failure mode because it is typically a long-running application. A developer who runs `setx` in a terminal, opens a new VS Code terminal tab expecting to see the new value, and finds the old state naturally assumes the `setx` failed. The command succeeded — the new terminal tab's shell simply inherited VS Code's launch-time environment. The diagnostic check: open a terminal that is **not** a child of VS Code (e.g., a standalone PowerShell window launched from the Start menu or `Win + R → powershell`) and verify `$env:VARNAME` there. If the value appears, `setx` worked correctly and the issue is purely propagation to the existing VS Code process tree. The authoritative fix is to close VS Code fully and reopen it. The same failure class applies to any long-running parent application — browser DevTools, Electron apps, terminal multiplexers — wherever a sub-process's environment was determined at the parent's launch rather than by the current system state.

# Claude Memory Compiler Setup

On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` system — the same daily-log-to-knowledge-base architecture this very knowledge base runs on — was installed to give Claude Code persistent memory across sessions. The repo was cloned to `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`, Python dependencies installed via `uv sync`, and the knowledge base directory structure (`daily/`, `knowledge/concepts/`, etc.) initialized. This system is Tier C of a three-tier Claude Code memory architecture; see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] for the full picture including Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook scratchpad). On 2026-06-13, a day-long failure caused by `claude-agent-sdk` version skew revealed an important operational maintenance pattern.

## Key Points

- Three global hooks were wired into `~/.claude/settings.json`: `session-start.py` (SessionStart), `session-end.py` (SessionEnd), and `pre-compact.py` (PreCompact).
- Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.
- All script invocations follow the `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler <script>` pattern, guaranteeing the correct virtualenv context regardless of the current working directory when a hook fires.
- Hook configuration changes are not picked up live — they require a full Claude Code restart (or a `/hooks` reload) before they take effect.
- After 6 PM local time, the `flush.py` background process automatically triggers `compile.py` to turn that day's daily log into knowledge articles, without manual intervention. Manual queries are also available via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/query.py "<question>"`.
- **The agent itself never receives a "session ending" notification** — SessionEnd and PreCompact are harness-level events; the harness runs the hook shell commands, not the agent. Teardown logic must live in the hook, not in agent-side instructions.
- **Version skew failure mode:** the memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk` to a specific version, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary. When the system Claude Code auto-updates (e.g., from 2.1.92 to 2.1.177), the bundled CLI in the venv falls behind and eventually cannot parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json`, causing every `flush.py` invocation to exit immediately with a non-zero code. Symptom: 100% FLUSH_ERROR rate after a Claude Code update, despite no changes to the memory compiler itself.
- **Fix for version skew:** `cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`. This upgrades only the `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and its bundled CLI to match the current system version without touching other pinned dependencies. Run this whenever FLUSH_ERRORs appear after a Claude Code auto-update.
- **Diagnostic caution:** do NOT invoke the bundled `claude.exe` CLI directly to diagnose version skew — it spawns a real nested agent session. Instead, inspect venv package metadata (e.g., `uv pip show claude-agent-sdk`) to check the installed version against the system CLI version.

## Details

The setup session focused on making the memory pipeline reliable rather than merely functional. The PATH issue with `uv` is a generalizable lesson for any Claude Code hook that shells out to a tool installed via `uv`, `pipx`, or similar user-local installers: hook processes may run with a minimal environment, so absolute paths (or explicit `PATH` exports) are safer than relying on the interactive shell's configuration. Similarly, the `uv run --directory` pattern avoids a whole class of "wrong virtualenv" bugs that would otherwise occur if a hook fires while Claude Code's working directory is some unrelated project.

Once restarted, the three hooks form a closed loop: `session-start.py` injects the current knowledge index and the most recent daily log into every new session's context (capped at 20,000 characters), `session-end.py` and `pre-compact.py` capture the raw conversation transcript and spawn a detached `flush.py` process, and `flush.py` decides what's worth appending to the day's daily log and, after 6 PM, kicks off `compile.py` to synthesize that log into structured `knowledge/` articles. PreCompact serves as a safety net for long sessions: in a session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, ensuring at least one compiled log exists even if the session later crashes before SessionEnd fires.

The 2026-06-13 version skew failure is operationally important. On that day, Claude Code auto-updated from approximately version 2.1.92 to 2.1.177 — 85 releases ahead — while the memory compiler's venv still bundled the older CLI via `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56`. The newer `~/.claude/settings.json` included hooks, settings, or schemas added after version 2.1.92 that the stale bundled CLI could not parse; every `flush.py` call exited on startup without processing the session. The failure was isolated entirely to the Tier C compile layer: Tier B (the `transcript-capture.js` Stop-hook) continued capturing sessions uninterrupted because it has no dependency on `claude-agent-sdk`. Twenty-four days of continuous Tier B logs and four sessions captured on the failure day itself confirmed the architectural independence. This means that during a version-skew failure, raw session context is preserved in Tier B transcripts and can be backfilled after the fix is applied. The `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync` fix is surgical — it upgrades only the affected package without touching other pinned dependencies — and is safe to apply at any time. A post-fix test flush verifies the fix before trusting that normal operation has resumed. See [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] for the architectural insight this failure demonstrated empirically.

# Google Workspace Cleanup via gws CLI (Drive Dedup + Gmail Organization)

On 2026-06-25, a Google Drive cleanup and Gmail inbox organization project was run through the Google Workspace CLI (`gws`), spanning duplicate-file deduplication, OAuth/auth-stability troubleshooting, Gmail signature setup, and inbox filtering for financial/receipt emails. The session established that duplicate detection by filename/metadata alone is unreliable — content-level diffing caught a false-positive duplicate group — and traced repeated OAuth session drops to an unpublished app.

## Key Points

- **Content-level verification before duplicate deletion:** filename/size heuristics are insufficient to confirm true duplicates. A "group 180" cover-letter set of three seemingly identical files contained one file with different mid-document text; content-level diffing caught the false positive. The same scrutiny was applied to video/audio "duplicates" flagged only by filename/size.
- **No Drive files deleted without an explicit verification step:** the user manually verified a sample before approving deletion; the verified duplicate-deletion plan was only executed after user confirmation.
- **OAuth session drops traced to an unpublished app:** repeated Google Workspace auth drops were root-caused to the `gws` app being unpublished. Publishing the app and confirming granted permissions resolved the recurring auth instability.
- **Gmail organization:** the Updates inbox held 23,000+ messages; a dedicated label/filter was set up to auto-sort receipts/financial-transaction emails away from Updates. A Gmail signature was also configured.
- **Working files consolidated** to a new folder at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\agy` for easier access; the user deferred remaining email-cleanup recommendations to Claude's discretion.

## Details

The governing principle of the session was conservatism around destructive operations, mirroring the safe-deletion discipline seen in other cleanup work. Rather than trusting the CLI's duplicate flags — which are derived from filename and metadata heuristics — the workflow inserted a mandatory content-verification step before any deletion. This caught a real false positive: a set of three cover-letter files that matched on name and size but differed in mid-document text. Had the deletion proceeded on heuristic matching alone, a genuinely distinct document would have been lost. The same content-level scrutiny was extended to video and audio files flagged as duplicates, where filename/size collisions are especially likely to be coincidental. This is a specific instance of the "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" pattern: the duplicate-flag is an intermediate proxy for actual file identity, and it fails precisely when files share superficial metadata but differ in content.

The OAuth instability was a separate thread. The `gws` CLI's Google Workspace session was dropping repeatedly, interrupting the cleanup work. The root cause was that the underlying OAuth app was in an unpublished state, which imposes shorter token lifetimes and re-consent requirements; publishing the app and re-confirming the granted scopes stabilized the session. On the Gmail side, the Updates category had accumulated 23,000+ messages, obscuring actionable content; a dedicated label plus filter was created to route receipts and financial-transaction emails out of Updates automatically, and a signature was configured. The user consolidated saved working files into a new `DEV\agy` folder and deferred the remaining Gmail loose-end recommendations to Claude's judgment, confirming "all good for now" with no outstanding follow-ups.

# $dev-sync Repo Sweep (2026-09-23 Clean Run)

`$dev-sync` is a Codex-invoked sweep that walks every repository under `Desktop\DEV`, pushes local commits, pulls incoming ones, and reports anomalies. The 2026-09-23 run was accepted as clean: 143 repos checked and pushed, 3 pulled incoming commits, none cloned or created, and no `.from-*` conflict files generated. It is the routine counterpart to the one-time staged migration described in [[concepts/dev-github-drive-migration-policy]] — the mechanism that keeps the migrated estate synchronized afterward.

## Key Points

- **Clean-run signature:** 143 repos checked and pushed, 3 with incoming commits pulled, 0 cloned or created, 0 `.from-*` conflict files. The absence of `.from-*` files is the sweep's primary conflict indicator — their presence means a two-machine divergence needed manual reconciliation.
- **Known benign exception:** `AthleticMedicineReviews` remains an empty unversioned folder and is expected to appear as such; a recurring non-defect that would otherwise read as a miss on every run.
- **The sweep feeds work selection.** With sync clean, the session picked up `PFF_Data_Project` per its `STATUS.md`: 2026 data covers graded weeks 0–3, the Parquet exchange is complete on both machines, nothing blocking. Per-repo `STATUS.md` files act as the resumable queue.
- **Sync health is reported separately from repo health.** The same day's `daily-backup` reported `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` and the memory compiler had 2 pending logs plus a stale compile lock reclaimed after 1531 minutes (~25.5 h) — failures in the automation layer that a clean DEV sweep does not cover.

## Details

The value of a sweep like `$dev-sync` is that it converts a 143-repo estate from something no one can hold in mind into a single pass/fail signal with a small set of named exceptions. Its output is only meaningful if the expected exceptions are documented — `AthleticMedicineReviews` as a permanently empty unversioned folder is exactly such a case, and recording it prevents a recurring benign finding from either being re-investigated each run or, worse, training the reader to ignore the anomaly section entirely. The `.from-*` conflict-file convention gives the sweep a cheap divergence detector: rather than attempting a merge across two machines, it materializes the incoming variant under a suffixed name and leaves reconciliation to a human, so "no `.from-*` files" is a positive statement that no repo diverged, not merely that no push failed.

The session's second observation is that a clean sweep in one layer says nothing about adjacent automation. The `daily-backup` job reported `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` — the backup declining to proceed because that repo was behind its remote — and the memory compiler had accumulated 2 pending logs behind a compile lock held for 1531 minutes before being reclaimed. A lock held over a day indicates a crashed or killed holder rather than legitimate contention, and the reclamation is the recovery path; the pending-log backlog is the visible cost. This is the same class of scheduled-job drift catalogued in [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]], where periodic health-check runs surface exactly these per-task escalations, and it reinforces that "sync is clean" and "the automation stack is healthy" are independent claims requiring independent checks.

# Connection: Claude Code Hook Environment ≠ Interactive Shell

## The Connection

On 2026-04-14, setting up `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` hooks required calling `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH` even when the user's interactive shell does — see [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]. ## Key Insight

Claude Code's hook runner is a minimal bash process, not the user's interactive shell. It does not inherit the user's `PATH` customizations, shell functions, aliases, or shell choice (PowerShell on Windows, zsh on macOS, etc.). Any tool or installer that generates hook commands by observing or targeting the interactive shell's environment will produce hooks that may work interactively but fail silently or noisily when Claude Code fires them.

The two incidents differ in their surface presentation — one is a missing binary (PATH), the other is incompatible shell syntax (PowerShell `&` in bash) — but both stem from the same assumption failure: "if it works in my terminal, it will work as a Claude Code hook." The preventive rule is consistent across both cases: normalize hook commands to their most portable form. Prefer absolute paths for binaries not guaranteed to be on a minimal bash `PATH`, and use POSIX shell syntax rather than shell-specific constructs. When in doubt, test the exact hook command under `bash -c "..."` in a fresh terminal (not the interactive one) to simulate the hook runner's environment.

# Connection: Install-Time Reference Capture Goes Stale When the Host Component Moves

## The Connection

The Claude memory compiler and memsearch are different tools serving the same Tier-C/Tier-A memory stack, and each suffered a day-plus outage from the *same structural failure class*: a subordinate tool captures a hard reference to a larger, independently-moving host component at install time, and that reference silently goes stale when the host updates or migrates underneath it. The memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56`, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary (2.1.92); when the system Claude Code auto-updated to 2.1.177, the stale bundled CLI could no longer parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json` and every `flush.py` exited non-zero. Memsearch embeds an absolute Python interpreter path in `memsearch.exe` at install time; when Python was migrated to a new path, the embedded reference became invalid and the binary failed at startup. Neither failure was a configuration error in the surrounding environment — the broken reference lived *inside the tool's own captured state*.

## Key Insight

The diagnostic trap is identical in both cases: the tool appears installed, its files exist, it is on `PATH`, yet it fails — and the error points at the host component (a CLI version mismatch, a missing Python path) rather than at the tool itself. The correct remediation in both is **re-synchronize the captured reference against the current host**, not adjust `PATH` or environment variables:

- **Memory compiler:** `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync` — a surgical re-pin of only the SDK (and its bundled CLI) to match the current system Claude Code, leaving other pinned deps untouched.
- **Memsearch:** reinstall into the new Python environment so the fresh interpreter path is re-embedded, then re-apply the flush patch and replace the stale shim.

The transferable lesson: any tool that *bundles or embeds* a version/path of a component it does not itself own has taken on a hidden maintenance obligation that comes due whenever that component moves. The failure is invisible until the host updates, it is silent (non-zero exit, no loud alarm), and it is un-diagnosable from documentation — it requires knowing that a reference was frozen at install time. This is the same staleness family as `setx` values captured by running processes and Task Scheduler's minimal PATH: a value snapshotted at one moment fails to track a later change to the world around it. The operational defense is to treat every host auto-update or migration as a trigger to re-verify (and re-sync) subordinate tools that pinned against it.

## Details

What makes this pairing more than "two tools broke" is that the two tools sit at *different layers of the same stack* yet fail the same way, which reveals the pattern is structural rather than incidental. The memory compiler is a Python application whose captured reference is a *bundled dependency version* (an SDK that in turn ships a CLI). Memsearch is a compiled binary whose captured reference is a *filesystem path to an interpreter*. Superficially unrelated — a semver pin versus a shebang path — but both are the act of freezing "the thing I depend on, as it exists right now" into the tool at install time. When Claude Code auto-updates or Python migrates, the frozen snapshot and the live host diverge, and the tool that trusted its snapshot dies. The 2026-06-17 discovery that a standard `.venv` (`pyvenv.cfg` referencing a removed `C:\Python314`) fails identically to memsearch confirms the class generalizes beyond either specific tool.

The two incidents also teach complementary halves of the same operational discipline. The memory-compiler failure teaches *when* to suspect it: a tool that worked yesterday and broke today with no change to itself, immediately after a host auto-update, is the fingerprint of install-time staleness — and the diagnostic caution (inspect venv package metadata rather than invoking the bundled `claude.exe`, which spawns a real nested session) mirrors memsearch's caution to reinstall rather than fiddle with PATH. The memsearch failure teaches *how* to recover durably: reinstalling produces a fresh, unmodified binary, so any local patch (the flush patch) must be documented and re-applied every time the captured reference is re-synced. Both point to the same maintenance posture — subordinate tools that pin against a moving host are not fire-and-forget; each host update is a scheduled re-sync waiting to happen, and the fix should be surgical (re-pin only the drifted reference) rather than a full environment rebuild.

# Baylor Load Simulator: Comparison View (Projected vs. Actual)

On 2026-05-12, a `ComparisonChart` component was designed and shipped for the [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-deployment]] app, overlaying projected and actual practice load on the existing `/practices/[id]/compare` page. The same session planned the chart's promotion from a per-practice subpage into a top-level `/comparison` navigation tab.

## Key Points

- `ComparisonChart` overlays "Projected" and "Actual" PL/Player values using dashed vs. solid lines, with red/green gap shading to highlight where actual load deviated from the plan, plus hover tooltips for per-period detail.
- The chart was deliberately scoped to a single metric (PL/Player); adding a second metric (PL/min) was explicitly rejected to keep the visualization focused.
- Promoting the comparison view to a top-level `/comparison` index route (alongside the existing `/reference` and `/admin` nav items) was confirmed as the next session's task - estimated at 30-45 minutes, with no database schema changes required.
- The chart's accuracy depends on the underlying Catapult sync/aggregation logic, which the same session found to have period-ordering issues - see [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]].
- Two lower-priority follow-ups were logged: a "practice-face seed cleanup" for scrimmage days, and a "scrimmage-vs-regular calibration view" to be built once the first fall-camp scrimmage provides real data to calibrate against.

## Details

The `ComparisonChart` is the first feature in the load simulator that visually juxtaposes a coach's planned ("projected") practice load against what Catapult GPS data actually recorded ("actual"), making over- and under-loading immediately visible via color-coded gap shading and dashed/solid line styling. This builds directly on the persistent navigation bar added during the app's initial Vercel deployment (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-deployment]]), which already links `/reference` and `/admin`; the planned `/comparison` index route would become a third top-level destination in that same nav bar, generalizing the existing per-practice `/practices/[id]/compare` view into a team-wide index.

The decision to keep the chart single-metric (PL/Player only, no PL/min) reflects a preference in this project for incremental, focused UI changes over comprehensive dashboards, consistent with the "no schema changes" framing given for the next session's nav work. Because the comparison view is the primary consumer of synced Catapult period data, building it surfaced a data-quality issue in the underlying sync logic - the same period type ("1 ON 1") appearing twice, non-adjacently, within a single practice - which is documented separately in [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]]. The two deferred follow-ups (scrimmage-day practice-face seed cleanup, and a scrimmage-vs-regular calibration view triggered by the first fall-camp scrimmage) are both framed as "revisit once more real data exists," echoing the same wait-for-data posture taken on the Catapult aggregation question.

# Extracting Gated Wistia Course Videos with yt-dlp

On 2026-09-24, a transcript and summary were extracted from a gated, Wistia-hosted course video ("Lab 3A: Kaigi Meeting Structure," from the Oldbull Performance *Running the Room* course) that offered no captions, no transcript option, and no direct file download. The working pattern turned out to be `yt-dlp` addressed with a `wistia:<id>` pseudo-URL, where the ID is read off the embedded player rather than the page URL. The session produced two artifacts — a timestamped machine-generated transcript draft and a summary — under `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\Codex\2026-09-24\can-x20\outputs\`.

## Key Points

- **A browser session cannot transcribe a video.** The Codex browser connection gives visual inspection only — no audio channel — and the Wistia player exposed neither caption tracks nor a transcript control, so there was no in-browser path to the content.
- **Chrome's built-in media download fails on streaming players.** Two attempts returned "Check internet connection," which is a misleading error: the player serves a streaming playlist rather than a direct MP4, so there is no single file for the browser to fetch.
- **The working invocation uses a Wistia pseudo-URL, not the page URL:** `.\yt-dlp.exe -f "best[ext=mp4]" -o "Lab 3A - Kaigi Meeting Structure.%(ext)s" "wistia:xc103yobe7"` — 247.62 MiB downloaded successfully. The standalone `yt-dlp.exe` was used on Windows, requiring no Python environment. The ID (`xc103yobe7`) must be pulled from the embedded player markup; the course page URL does not contain it.
- **Files downloaded via PowerShell never appear in Chrome's download history.** Verification belongs in File Explorer, not `Ctrl+J`; the failed browser-download entries still sitting in Chrome history were unrelated leftovers and actively misleading as evidence.
- **A page-notes summary is not a video summary.** The first summary produced was synthesized from the lesson's written notes rather than the video's spoken content; the corrective rule is to state explicitly which source an artifact summarizes.
- **Machine transcripts are drafts.** The generated transcript contains speech-recognition errors and must be cleaned before the Kaigi content is used for anything staff-facing.

## Details

The escalation path in this session is the reusable part. Three access tiers were tried in order of decreasing convenience: watch/transcribe in the browser (impossible — no audio, no captions), use the browser's native media download (fails on streaming playlists), and finally reach past the browser entirely with a dedicated downloader. The two rejected alternatives at the third tier were screen recording with system audio and simply asking Oldbull for the source file or caption track; `yt-dlp` was chosen because it needs no real-time capture and no counterparty response. This is the same substitute-a-primitive move that recurs whenever an intermediate layer is unreliable: rather than debugging why Chrome reports a connection error, drop to a tool that speaks the streaming protocol directly.

Two of the session's lessons are about evidence rather than extraction. Chrome's download history is scoped to Chrome's own downloads, so a file fetched by a PowerShell-invoked binary is invisible there — and because the earlier failed browser attempts *did* leave entries, the history actively suggested failure after the download had already succeeded. The correct check is the filesystem. Similarly, the first summary was drawn from the lesson's written page notes, which read as plausibly on-topic but describe a different artifact than the video; labeling the provenance of a summary ("this summarizes the page notes" versus "this summarizes the audio") is what makes the distinction visible to a downstream reader. Both are instances of verifying at the layer that owns the state rather than at a convenient surface that merely appears to report on it.

# Two-Machine Split Workday and Closeout (2026-09-24)

On 2026-09-24 the working day was deliberately split across two machines — Windows during the day, Mac in the evening — and closed out from the Windows laptop with a structured sign-off: push every context repo, consolidate Tier A memory under its character cap, and write a handoff of record naming everything the Mac still owed. The day also carried an S2 data migration to Google Drive and eight merged PRs. The handoff lives at `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\global-memory\handoffs\2026-09-24-machine-split.md`.

## Key Points

- **Unpushed work blocks sign-off.** Four context repos — `global-memory`, `dotclaude`, `claude-memory-compiler`, and `SecondBrain` — were committed and pushed even though three carried changes left behind by *other* sessions. Rather than leaving them dirty or deferring, the closeout named the foreign changes explicitly in its report and pushed them.
- **Tier A memory is consolidated by displacement, not growth.** `MEMORY.md` sits under a 2,500-character cap; adding a "Machine split (9/24)" line required removing the existing "Data pulls" line, landing the file at 2,378 characters. A capped memory file forces an explicit eviction decision on every addition.
- **Cross-machine delegation is unverifiable from the delegating side.** Instructions sent to a Mac session cannot report back, so every Mac-side item is recorded as "unconfirmed" until the user verifies on that machine — including a backup plist moved to 21:00, to be checked with `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup | grep -A4 -i calendar`.
- **The handoff enumerates per-machine next actions, not a merged list.** Windows: run `ritual-check.ps1 -Notify` once, then `Enable-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'KeystoneOS-Rituals'`. Mac: rsync `ol_scores.csv` and `team_scores.csv` from `~/DEV/S2_Evaluation/data/` to the Drive S2 folder, `launchctl bootout …/com.keystone.rituals`, and a first `export_snapshot.py` run in each of three pull repos.
- **Open decisions and known failures were carried forward rather than silently dropped:** whether to add a Windows 17:30 auto-push of the context repos; fixing the failing "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" task via `/claude-stack-doctor`; and pointing Perch's Windows reads at the Parquet snapshots.

## Details

The closeout's governing rule is that durable state must be durable on *both* machines before the day is declared finished, which makes pushing the context repos non-negotiable. This produced a deliberate reversal of the earlier practice of deferring commits in a dirty tree: three of the four repos held work authored by other concurrent sessions, and the choice was to commit and push them anyway while naming each foreign change in the report. The reasoning is that the alternative — leaving them dirty — guarantees the next session on either machine inherits an ambiguous working tree, whereas pushing with attribution costs only a slightly noisier history. The transparency step (naming whose change went along for the ride) is what makes the blanket push defensible; see [[concepts/scoped-commit-in-dirty-working-tree]] for the scoped-commit discipline this consciously departs from and the four-day deferral cost that motivated the change.

The machine split also exposes a structural asymmetry: the Windows session can *issue* work to the Mac but cannot *observe* it. Every Mac-side item therefore enters the handoff in an unconfirmed state with an explicit verification command attached, so the user — the only agent present on both machines — can close the loop. The same asymmetry appeared within the Windows session itself when a direct check of the S2 Drive folder was refused by the permission layer (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]) and when a background watch on that folder was reaped under memory pressure (see [[concepts/background-job-reaped-memory-pressure]]); in all three cases the honest output is a named gap rather than an assumed success. The cross-machine data plumbing being established — `export_snapshot.py` in each pull repo producing Parquet snapshots that the other machine reads — is the structural answer to this: rather than each host reaching into the other's live data, both read committed snapshots, which is also why Perch's Windows reads are queued to be repointed at them.

# Background Shell Jobs Reaped Under System Memory Pressure

On 2026-09-24, a long-running background job — a watch waiting for S2 data to appear on Google Drive — was terminated by Claude Code because the Windows laptop was critically low on memory. The termination was a resource-reclamation action, not a command failure, and the accompanying notification explicitly instructed that the job not be restarted. It was left dead, and the dependent check was reported as unconfirmed instead.

## Key Points

- **The harness may reap an idle session's background jobs to reclaim system memory.** The trigger is host memory pressure, independent of the job's own correctness or progress.
- **A reap notification is not a debugging signal.** There is no failing command to diagnose, no exit code to interpret, and no log to inspect — treating it as a bug wastes effort and invites a harmful retry.
- **Restarting on your own initiative is explicitly discouraged.** The notification carries that instruction, and relaunching the same memory-consuming watch on a host that just ran out of memory reproduces the condition that caused the kill.
- **The correct downstream behavior is to report the resulting gap.** With the watch gone, the S2 Drive state was simply unknown; the session recorded it as unverified rather than asserting or re-attempting a result.
- **Indefinite waits are the wrong shape for an in-session job.** A watch that blocks until an external event occurs has no bounded lifetime, making it the most likely candidate for reaping and a natural fit for a scheduled task instead.

## Details

Background-task notifications in Claude Code are ambiguous by default: the same channel reports genuine command failures, false-positive nonzero exits, and — as here — harness-initiated terminations. Distinguishing them matters because the correct response differs completely. A real failure calls for reading the log and fixing the cause; a false-positive exit calls for reconciling against on-disk artifacts, which is the lesson of [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]; a memory-pressure reap calls for doing nothing to the job and instead adjusting what is claimed downstream. The distinguishing evidence in this case was the notification's own text naming critically low memory and directing that the job not be restarted, which is a stronger signal than any exit code.

The structural lesson reinforces a limit already documented for this environment: work whose duration is unbounded does not belong inside a session. A watch waiting on an external filesystem event has no natural completion, so it accumulates the risk of session teardown, compaction, and — as seen here — resource reclamation, all of which kill it without completing the thing it was waiting for. The durable alternative is a scheduled job that polls and escalates on its own cadence, which is precisely the relocation applied to memsearch's hours-long reindex. In the immediate term, the session took the honest path: because the watch was the only mechanism that would have confirmed the S2 data landed on Drive, and a direct folder check was separately refused by the permission layer, the outcome was recorded as an unconfirmed item in the day's handoff rather than an assumed success.

# Permission Layer Blocking Athlete-Data Verification

On 2026-09-24, a direct check of the S2 data folder on Google Drive was refused by Claude Code's permission layer because the directory listing itself included an athlete-named file. No workaround was attempted; the session reported the block, told the user that a permission rule would be needed to allow such confirmations in future, and recorded the migration's landing state as unconfirmed. The episode is a clean example of an athlete-data guardrail working as designed while imposing a real verification cost.

## Key Points

- **A filename can be the protected content.** The block was triggered not by reading a file's contents but by *listing* a directory, because athlete names appear in the file names — so directory metadata is itself identifiable data under the policy.
- **No circumvention was attempted.** Rather than rerouting through a different tool, a shell glob, or a partial listing, the refusal was accepted and surfaced. Guardrails around athlete and health data are treated as policy, not as obstacles to engineer around.
- **The remedy is an explicit permission rule, not an ad-hoc override.** The user was told that allowing future confirmations requires adding a rule — a deliberate, reviewable configuration change rather than a one-off bypass.
- **The cost is a verification gap, and the gap must be named.** Combined with the same session's reaped background watch, the block left no path to confirm the S2 data had landed on Drive; the outcome was carried into the handoff as unconfirmed rather than assumed.
- **This is the enforcement surface of an existing policy.** The destination-split rule already routes athlete-identifiable data to Drive only and never to GitHub; the permission layer is where that intent becomes mechanical.

## Details

The interesting property of this block is where the sensitivity lives. Most data-governance rules assume the payload is the risk and the path is neutral, which is why gitignoring a `data/` directory is usually sufficient — the files stay out of the remote, and naming them is harmless. Here the inverse held: the request was a listing, the payload was never read, and the identifiable information was carried entirely in the file names. Any tool that enumerates a directory therefore handles athlete-identifiable data, which means the guardrail has to sit at the enumeration boundary rather than only at the read boundary. That is broader than it first appears and explains why an apparently innocuous `ls`-equivalent triggered a refusal.

The response pattern is the transferable part. A blocked operation creates pressure to find an equivalent path — a different tool, a narrower glob, a count instead of a listing — and each of those would technically satisfy the request while defeating the rule's purpose. Declining to look for one, and instead escalating to "a permission rule would be needed," keeps the decision with the person who owns the policy and leaves an auditable record of what was and was not verified. The cost is accepted honestly: the S2 Drive confirmation simply did not happen, and because the background watch that would otherwise have reported the arrival was reaped for memory pressure in the same session, the item left the day as an explicit unknown. An unconfirmed item in a handoff is a better artifact than a confident claim produced by working around a guardrail.

# Connection: Confirmation Must Come From the Layer That Owns the State

## The Connection

Four separate sessions hit the same wall from different directions: the place where a result was *requested* was not the place where the result actually *lived*, so the requesting side could not confirm it. On 2026-07-21 a PR merge appeared to fail because the local main checkout could not swap branches, while the squash-merge had in fact landed on GitHub — the remote owned the state ([[concepts/worktree-remote-merge-verification]]). On 2026-07-18 a background R pull reported exit 1 while its output files sat complete on disk — the filesystem owned the state ([[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). On 2026-09-24 a Windows session delegated work to a Mac session that structurally cannot report back, and separately lost the one watch that would have confirmed a Drive upload while being refused permission to look at the folder directly ([[concepts/machine-split-workday-closeout]], [[concepts/background-job-reaped-memory-pressure]], [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]).

## Key Insight

The instinct in all four cases is to trust the nearest available signal — the local checkout, the exit code, the absence of a complaint from the delegated machine — because it is the signal that happens to be in hand. Each of those signals is a *report about* the state rather than the state itself, and each is generated by a layer that does not own the thing being asked about. A local worktree does not own the remote's branch graph; a process's exit status does not own the bytes it wrote; a session on one machine owns nothing on another.

This produces two distinct correct behaviors depending on whether the owning layer is reachable. When it is, query it directly and ignore the proxy: check `gh` or the remote branch, list the output artifacts, read the file. When it is not — a second machine with no return channel, a folder a permission rule forbids listing — the only honest output is an explicitly *unconfirmed* item, paired with the exact command the party who can reach the owning layer should run. The 2026-09-24 handoff does this literally, attaching `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup | grep -A4 -i calendar` to the Mac plist change rather than recording it as done. The failure mode this forecloses is the most expensive one available: a confident false claim of completion, which is strictly worse than an admitted gap because nothing downstream will ever re-check it.

## Evidence

- 2026-07-21: the PR merge "failed" locally because the main checkout owned main; the GitHub squash-merge had landed and synced via fast-forward pull — verify the remote, not the local swap.
- 2026-07-18: a background task's exit-1 notification was a false positive for the SpeedProfiling R pull; reconciliation against on-disk artifacts and logs established success.
- 2026-09-24: "Cross-machine instructions sent to a Mac session cannot report back — anything delegated there is 'unconfirmed' until the user verifies on that machine." The Mac items were written with verification commands attached.
- 2026-09-24: the S2 Drive confirmation was doubly unreachable — the watch job was reaped for memory pressure, and a direct listing was refused because it contained an athlete-named file — and was reported as an unknown rather than inferred.

# Scoped Commit in a Dirty Working Tree (dotclaude Repo)

When the 2026-09-19 hook fix landed in `~/.claude/settings.json`, the change was deliberately left uncommitted and handed to the user with an exact path-scoped command. The reason was the state of the surrounding working tree: `~/.claude` is the synced `erash11/dotclaude` repository, and it carried unrelated uncommitted work — a `UserPromptSubmit` skill-router hook from a separate thread, plus dirty session transcripts. Committing the repair required staging one file by path rather than the whole tree. The commit was finally made and pushed on 2026-09-23, and by 2026-09-24 the practice had shifted again: the day's closeout pushed the whole tree with the foreign changes named in the report.

## Key Points

- **The prescribed command stages a single file:** `git -C ~/.claude add settings.json && git commit -m "Hooks: drop the unguarded Mac-path dcg duplicate" && git push`. The `-C` flag targets the repo without changing the working directory, and naming the path avoids sweeping in adjacent changes.
- **A dirty tree makes a blanket commit unsafe, not merely untidy.** In-flight work from another thread would be committed half-finished, and transcript churn would be pushed to a shared remote alongside a one-line config fix.
- **The commit was deferred to the user rather than performed** — the change touched a synced personal-config repo with third-party-authored pending work in it.
- **Deferral has a measured cost.** The handoff was not executed until 2026-09-23, four days later; in the interim the duplicate hook stayed in `HEAD`, the Mac kept double-firing, and one Windows session logged 49 `PreToolUse` errors before the fix was pushed.
- **The 2026-09-24 closeout adopted the opposite resolution: commit with attribution.** `global-memory`, `dotclaude`, `claude-memory-compiler`, and `SecondBrain` were all committed and pushed even though three carried other sessions' changes, with each foreign change named in the closeout report — on the rule that unpushed work blocks sign-off.
- **Transcripts are routine noise in this repo.** Session records accumulate as working-tree changes continuously, so `~/.claude` is dirty by default — path-scoped commits are the normal mode there, not an exceptional accommodation.

## Details

The general rule this instance supports is that the appropriate staging granularity is a function of the repository's baseline cleanliness. In a project repo whose tree is clean between tasks, `git add -A` is a reasonable default and an unexpected extra file is itself a useful signal. In a configuration or state repo that is dirty as a matter of course — one holding transcripts, caches, machine-local scratch, or work from concurrent threads — the same command silently bundles unrelated content into every commit, destroying the history's usefulness for bisecting or reverting a specific change. `~/.claude` is squarely in the second category, which is why the remediation was written as an explicit single-path stage.

The deferral decision is separable from the scoping decision and rests on different grounds, and the 2026-09-23 outcome allows it to be graded. The repair itself was verified on 2026-09-19 — JSON validated, one hook remaining in the array, all 22 top-level keys intact, backup written — so the hesitation was not about correctness of the edit; it was about authority over a synced personal repo containing another thread's unfinished hook work. The risk recorded at the time was concrete and materialized: for four days `HEAD` carried a `settings.json` whose `PreToolUse` array ran `dcg` twice per tool call on the Mac and errored on every matching call on Windows. The lesson is that scoping and deferring are independent choices: path-scoping is what makes a commit safe in a dirty tree, and once the scoped command is known and the edit verified, deferring it further buys nothing while leaving the defect live on every synced host. See [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]] for the defect and its eventual push.

The 2026-09-24 closeout resolved the residual tension in a third way, which is worth recording as a deliberate policy shift rather than a lapse. Facing four context repos of which three held other sessions' changes, it neither deferred nor path-scoped: it committed and pushed everything and *named the foreign changes in the report*. The justification is that a two-machine split makes unpushed work actively dangerous — the other host will start from the remote — so the closeout rule "unpushed work blocks sign-off" outranks history hygiene. Transparency does the work that scoping did previously: the cost of a mixed commit is that nobody knows what went into it, and enumerating the borrowed changes removes that cost without leaving the tree dirty. The resulting guidance is conditional rather than absolute — path-scope when a single verified fix must land cleanly and the rest of the tree can wait, push-with-attribution when another machine is about to pull and nothing may be left behind.

# DEV Project Migration to GitHub + Google Drive (Destination-Split Policy)

On 2026-09-14, a staged full-DEV migration moved all Codex and Claude projects to durable remote storage, governed by a destination-split policy that routes each artifact type to GitHub, Google Drive, or neither based on sensitivity and size. The audit at migration start counted 142 local repos with `erash11` remotes, 144 GitHub repos (141 private / 3 public), and none ahead of remote; Google Drive was mounted at `G:\My Drive` with `_DRIVE` mapping to `00_Primary_Storage_Drive`. On 2026-09-24 the policy entered an operational phase: the S2 evaluation data was migrated to Drive and a Parquet-snapshot exchange layer was stood up so two machines could share data without reaching into each other's live working trees.

## Key Points

- **Destination split by artifact type:** code / docs / `AGENTS.md` / `STATUS.md` → GitHub; large datasets, vendor exports, installers, and proprietary files → Google Drive; athlete-identifiable or health data → Drive only (never GitHub); raw conversation transcripts → Drive backup (never in project repos); credentials and `.env` files → neither destination; sanitized memory and handoff summaries → private GitHub context repos.
- **Working repos stay local:** live Git working directories remain under `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`. Google Drive holds external data and archives, not live working repos.
- **Intentional public/local exceptions:** `Travel_Map`, `SportScienceResearchRepo`, and `JumpReporting` remain intentionally public; `DexaProject` stays local/Drive-only due to sensitive athlete data and is never pushed to GitHub.
- **Codex history not durably backed up:** Codex conversation history is preserved locally under `C:\Users\eric_rash\.codex\sessions\` but is NOT in GitHub and NOT independently backed up off-device — a remaining gap.
- **Raw backups are themselves sensitive:** raw conversation backups contain athlete names, medical context, and historical credentials, so the Drive archive must stay private and unshared — the backup inherits the sensitivity of the most sensitive content it captures.
- **Snapshot exchange, not live cross-reads (2026-09-24):** each pull repo runs `export_snapshot.py` to emit Parquet snapshots that the other machine consumes; the Mac rsyncs `ol_scores.csv` and `team_scores.csv` from `~/DEV/S2_Evaluation/data/` into the Drive S2 folder, and Perch's Windows reads are queued to be repointed at the snapshots rather than at live sources.
- **The Drive-only rule is enforced at the tool layer, and that costs verifiability (2026-09-24):** a direct listing of the S2 Drive folder was refused because the listing itself contains an athlete-named file, leaving the migration's arrival unconfirmed rather than verified.

## Details

The migration's governing principle is that destination is a function of both size and sensitivity, not a single default. Ordinary code and documentation flow to GitHub where version history and collaboration matter; bulky or proprietary binaries (datasets, vendor exports, installers) go to Google Drive to keep repositories lean; and anything athlete-identifiable or health-related is confined to Drive-only storage so it never enters a Git remote at all. Credentials and `.env` files are excluded from both remotes entirely. Sanitized memory and handoff summaries occupy a fourth lane — private GitHub "context repos" — allowing durable, version-controlled continuity documents without exposing raw sensitive material. This mirrors the athlete-data-stays-local convention already established in Baylor's sports-tech pipelines (see [[concepts/kinexon-volleyball-tracking-project]] and [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]), where `data/` directories are gitignored so athlete-level data never leaves the machine.

Seven remaining Claude Cowork projects (S2 Cognition, WebApps, PlayerProfiles, StaffProject_BE, Post Season Analysis, UPskilling, PersonalKnowledgeManagement) were queued for migration via a `/migrate-project-to-disk` command and later reported complete in a resume checkpoint pending verification. Several follow-ups remained open: confirming that `Ath_Medicine`, `Baylor_Exposure_Data`, and `Risk_Stratification_Engine` contain no identifiable athlete/health data before their GitHub state is trusted; resolving `_INBOX` changes (a modified `recv.py`, two untracked closeout scripts, and five recovered Python utilities from `agent-skills/_recovered-from-codex/`); a guarded Windows skills v2 sync blocked on an absent `.sync-v2-ready` marker with divergent agent/Codex skill copies to reconcile; and stale documentation (`_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md` still claiming 7 Cowork projects remain, and a stale root "36 `.from-windows` files" item). Optional cleanup included removing a 3.2 GB `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\Codex` scratch folder and duplicate clones under `Desktop\DEV\_to_delete\2026-09-14_dup_clones`. Key final commits: DEV router `847bfb9`, `_INBOX` migration handoff `c7e0326`, Claude config `9e807eb`, global memory `b59bf55`, recovered agent utilities `4e00e86`.

The 2026-09-24 machine-split day exercised the policy in two instructive ways. First, once data lives on Drive rather than in a repo, two machines working the same projects need a defined exchange format; the answer adopted was per-repo `export_snapshot.py` runs producing Parquet snapshots, with each host reading the committed snapshot instead of the other host's live data — a read-only, reproducible handoff that keeps the Drive copy authoritative and avoids the divergence problems that plague direct cross-machine reads. Second, the Drive-only rule for athlete data proved to be enforced mechanically and more broadly than the written policy suggests: the permission layer refused a mere *directory listing* of the S2 folder because athlete names appear in file names, meaning identifiable data lives in the metadata as well as the payload (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]). No workaround was attempted, so the cost was accepted as an explicit verification gap in the day's handoff — the guardrail behaving correctly, at the price of not being able to confirm from that session that the migration landed.

entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`; the `alexandria` and `requestId` parameters describe batching, retries, errors and provider terms. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Identifies one logical Alexandria execution; generated when omitted and returned with the result. Repeated attempts of the identical payload require the same ID. A new ID cannot reconcile a pending or uncertain execution. A caller-supplied ID supports recovery if no response is received. Errors relay a code and may include chargeId. request_in_flight (409) means the execution is pending; request_unresolved (503) requires reconciliation under the same ID; duplicate_request (409) means the ID belongs to a different payload; unknown_provider (404), insufficient_credits (402) and billing_unavailable (503) mean nothing executed.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. nextTool identifies access to retained results without repeating a successful provider call. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. THIRD_PARTY_DATA_TERMS_REQUIRED (403) means execution is blocked by provider terms, with requiresAction.url for review by an organization admin. Through this tool, terms/show displays the agreement and terms/accept records acceptance; acceptance requires explicit user authorization for the reviewed version and digest and confirmed:true. A data request does not authorize acceptance. Provider execution remains blocked until acceptance is confirmed.

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
